analysis.one_liner: Repeals all federal and state energy-efficiency standards for appliances and equipment.
analysis.headline: With zero cosponsors, the bill died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the Department of Energy's power to set efficiency standards for refrigerators, air conditioners, water heaters, and other appliances, and repeal every standard already on the books. It would also bar states from setting their own efficiency or water-savings rules and nullify the ones they have. The result would be fewer requirements for manufacturers, and appliances that use more energy and water in homes and businesses.
analysis.who_benefits: Appliance and equipment manufacturers would be the main beneficiaries: they would no longer have to meet federal efficiency minimums, follow federal test procedures, or design products around state rules. Retailers and consumers who want maximally powerful or cheaper-up-front products would also have more choices, since some products currently excluded by minimum standards could return to the market.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the entire federal energy conservation standards program, removing minimum efficiency requirements for consumer and commercial products and eliminating DOE's authority to set new ones [S2][S3].

It voids every state efficiency and water-efficiency standard and prohibits any state or federal agency from adopting or continuing one, freeing manufacturers from a patchwork of state rules [S2][S3].
It replaces federal test procedures with 'generally accepted industry testing procedures,' letting industry norms govern how products are measured [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Households and businesses would bear higher utility bills over time, because the appliances available to them would use more energy and water than under the repealed standards. State governments would lose authority they currently use to protect their residents' energy costs. The wider public would bear increased energy consumption and the emissions that come with it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households, through higher energy and water bills

drawbacks.text: Without federal minimums, the average appliance on store shelves would use more energy, raising electricity and water bills for ordinary households over the life of the product — a cost that would fall hardest on people who cannot afford premium high-efficiency models [S2].
The bill strips states of their own authority to set efficiency and water rules, nullifying existing state standards even where state residents might want them [S2][S3].

A good-faith objection in its favor: federal standards impose compliance and testing costs on manufacturers, which can be passed into prices and can exclude niche products some consumers prefer. The bill's supporters framed this as letting the market rather than government decide [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Manufacturers would save compliance costs, and those savings would flow partly to consumers up front. But the repealed standards are designed to pay for themselves over an appliance's life through lower utility bills, so the likely net effect for most households is a higher total cost of ownership plus higher national energy use. Losing state standards compounds the downside for consumers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to committee, then to a subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended — no hearing, no vote, no movement.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Burgess introduced the bill on February 9, 2016, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the same day [S1][S5].
On February 12, 2016, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power, where no further action was ever taken [S5].
The bill drew no cosponsors at all, and it never received a hearing or floor vote before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary consumers and state governments are better off: the federal and state appliance efficiency standards that lower utility bills stayed on the books because the bill died in committee. Manufacturers who wanted relief from efficiency requirements did not get it.

for.name: Rep. Michael Burgess
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal federal and state energy-efficiency standards.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Energy and Power Subcommittee and took no further action; the bill never received a markup or a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so no party breakdown exists; the only action on record was the Republican sponsor's introduction and referral [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would free manufacturers from federal efficiency minimums, federal test procedures, and state rules, cutting their compliance costs. The saving to them is the mirror image of higher energy and water bills for households that buy the less efficient products this would allow [S2][S3].

States would lose the power to set their own efficiency and water-savings standards, and existing state standards would be nullified — removing a tool states use to lower residents' utility costs [S2][S3].

Repealing efficiency standards would increase energy and water demand, but it would also remove the certainty that comes with uniform federal rules and undermine the efficiency programs many utilities use to manage load growth.
